s:
Under Article 72 of the Constitution, the President may exercise the power of pardon in which of the following cases?
1. Sentences awarded by a court-martial
2. Offences against a law relating to a matter within the Union executive power
3. All cases involving a death sentence
4. Sentences imposed under State laws in every case
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
x: Article 72 covers court-martial sentences, offences against Union laws and all death sentences. It does not cover sentences under State laws in every case.
tq: Separate the three constitutional grounds from the overbroad State-law statement.
sec: Pardoning power - Article 72, forms and nature

s: Which one of the following best describes a pardon?
o: Temporary stay of execution of a sentence
Reduction in the period of sentence without altering its character
Substitution of a lighter form of punishment
Removal of both the sentence and the conviction
x: A pardon removes both the sentence and the conviction and frees the person from all punishment.
tq: Distinguish the complete relief of pardon from the partial relief provided by other forms.
sec: Pardoning power - Article 72, forms and nature

s: The substitution of a lighter form of punishment for a heavier punishment is known as:
o: Reprieve
Remission
Commutation
Respite
x: Commutation substitutes a lighter form of punishment, such as changing death sentence to rigorous imprisonment.
tq: Test the exact meaning of closely related legal terms.
sec: Pardoning power - Article 72, forms and nature

s: With reference to the President's pardoning power, which of the following statements is correct?
o: It is exercised on ministerial advice and is confined to the matters covered by Article 72(1)(a) to (c) and Union executive matters.
It is exercised independently of ministerial advice.
Amnesty is expressly included among the forms specified in Article 72.
It extends to every matter falling exclusively within State executive authority.
x: The President exercises the power on ministerial advice. Its constitutional scope is confined to Article 72(1)(a) to (c) and Union executive matters; amnesty is outside Article 72.
tq: Watch for the wrong-authority and overextension traps in constitutional powers.
sec: Pardoning power - Article 72, forms and nature

s: Which case held that the President may examine the evidence afresh while exercising the pardoning power, but that the convict has no right to an oral hearing?
o: Krishna Kumar Singh case
D.C. Wadhwa case
Epuru Sudhakar case
Kehar Singh case
x: In Kehar Singh (1989), the Supreme Court held that the President may examine the evidence afresh, but there is no right to an oral hearing.
tq: Link the judicial holding to the correct case name and year.

s: In which of the following circumstances may the exercise of the pardoning power be subjected to judicial review according to the principle laid down in Epuru Sudhakar (2006)?
o: When the decision is mala fide, arbitrary or based on irrelevant or extraneous grounds
Whenever the court disagrees with the quantum of punishment
Never, because clemency is a purely political power
Only when the convict has not been given an oral hearing
x: Epuru Sudhakar held that clemency may be reviewed when it is mala fide, arbitrary or based on irrelevant or extraneous considerations.
tq: Identify the limited grounds of judicial review instead of assuming total immunity or full appellate review.

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Articles 72 and 161:
1. The President may pardon a death sentence, whereas the Governor cannot pardon a death sentence.
2. The Governor may suspend, remit or commute a death sentence.
3. The Governor possesses the power to pardon a court-martial sentence.
4. Article 72 primarily relates to Union laws, while Article 161 relates to State laws.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. The Governor has no power to pardon a death sentence or a court-martial sentence; statement 3 is false.
tq: Compare the two constitutional powers by law covered, death sentence and court-martial competence.

s: Parliament can promulgate an Ordinance under Article 123 only when:
o: either House of Parliament is not in session and the President is satisfied that immediate action is necessary
the Supreme Court authorises the President to do so
the Council of States alone recommends immediate legislation
both Houses of Parliament are dissolved
x: An Ordinance may be promulgated when either House is not in session and the President is satisfied, on ministerial advice, that immediate action is necessary.
tq: Combine both mandatory conditions instead of treating dissolution as the sole requirement.

s: Which of the following statements regarding an Ordinance promulgated under Article 123 is correct?
o: It remains valid even if it violates Fundamental Rights.
It cannot amend or repeal an existing Act.
It has the force of an Act of Parliament while it remains operative.
It can never operate retrospectively.
x: An Ordinance has the force of an Act and may be retrospective or amend or repeal an Act, subject to constitutional limitations. It becomes void if beyond Parliament's competence or inconsistent with Fundamental Rights.
tq: Reject absolute limitations and identify the legal effect of an Ordinance.

s: An Ordinance promulgated under Article 123 ordinarily ceases to operate:
o: six months after promulgation in every case
only when the President expressly withdraws it
six weeks after the earlier date of reassembly of Parliament
six weeks after the later date of reassembly of Parliament
x: An Ordinance ceases six weeks after the later date on which the two Houses reassemble. It may end earlier if disapproved or withdrawn.
tq: Focus on the later reassembly date and distinguish the ordinary period from the maximum possible life.

s: Which one of the following is NOT a constitutionally permissible limitation on an Ordinance?
o: It may be issued even when both Houses are in session if the President considers it convenient.
It must not violate Fundamental Rights.
It must satisfy the constitutional requirement of immediate action.
It must not be beyond Parliament's legislative competence.
x: An Ordinance cannot be promulgated when Parliament is in session. The other options describe applicable constitutional requirements or limitations.
tq: Find the statement that reverses the basic precondition for ordinance-making.

s: The power to promulgate Ordinances under Articles 123 and 213 was made non-justiciable by the:
o: 38th Constitutional Amendment
42nd Constitutional Amendment
44th Constitutional Amendment
24th Constitutional Amendment
x: The 38th Amendment Act, 1975 made the satisfaction under Articles 123, 213 and 352 non-justiciable. The 44th Amendment later undid this change.
tq: Discriminate between the amendment that created and the amendment that reversed the legal position.

s: Which constitutional amendment undid the non-justiciability introduced by the 38th Amendment in respect of the satisfaction under Articles 123, 213 and 352?
o: 44th Amendment, 1978
24th Amendment, 1971
42nd Amendment, 1976
38th Amendment, 1975
x: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 reversed the non-justiciability introduced by the 38th Amendment.
tq: Use the amendment sequence to avoid confusing the original change with its reversal.

s: The Supreme Court described repeated re-promulgation of Ordinances without placing them before the legislature as a fraud on the Constitution in:
o: D.C. Wadhwa
State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu
Kehar Singh
Epuru Sudhakar
x: In D.C. Wadhwa (1987), repeated re-promulgation without placing Ordinances before the legislature was characterised as a fraud on the Constitution.
tq: Match the distinctive judicial phrase with the case that first articulated it.

s:
Consider the following statements about Krishna Kumar Singh (2017):
1. Re-promulgation of an Ordinance may constitute a fraud on the Constitution.
2. Laying the Ordinance before the legislature is mandatory.
3. The President's satisfaction is completely beyond judicial review.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Krishna Kumar Singh held that re-promulgation can be a fraud on the Constitution and that laying before the legislature is mandatory. It also recognised that the satisfaction is open to judicial review, making statement 3 false.
tq: Use the judicial-review statement as the discriminator among otherwise correct holdings.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Absolute veto — Indian President has no such power
Suspensive veto — Indian President may return a non-money Bill, but must assent if it is repassed
Pocket veto — Bill must be decided within ten days
Qualified veto — Indian President may override Parliament by a two-thirds majority
x: A suspensive veto permits return of a non-money Bill; if Parliament repasses it, with or without amendment, the President must assent. The Constitution does not prescribe a time limit for the pocket veto, and qualified veto is not held by the Indian President.
tq: Separate the four veto types by their effect and by whether the Indian President possesses them.
sec: Veto types - which the Indian President holds (Article 111)

s: Under Article 111, the President may do which of the following in relation to a non-money Bill?
o: Return it repeatedly until Parliament withdraws it
Assent, withhold assent or return it for reconsideration
Refer it compulsorily to the Supreme Court
Only assent or withhold assent, but never return it
x: Article 111 permits the President to assent to, withhold assent to, or return a non-money Bill for reconsideration.
tq: Recall the three textual alternatives in Article 111 and apply the money-Bill exception separately.
sec: Veto types - which the Indian President holds (Article 111)

s:
The absolute veto of the President may ordinarily operate in respect of which of the following situations?
1. A private member's Bill
2. A Government Bill when the Council of Ministers has resigned before assent
3. A Constitutional Amendment Bill
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Absolute veto may apply to a private member's Bill and to a Government Bill when the Cabinet resigns before assent. A Constitutional Amendment Bill must receive assent.
tq: Apply the veto type to the special categories of Bills rather than to ordinary Bills generally.
sec: Veto types - which the Indian President holds (Article 111)

s: A pocket veto means that the President:
o: withholds assent permanently through an express order
rejects only Money Bills without recording reasons
returns a Bill once and then must assent if it is repassed
neither assents to, rejects nor returns the Bill, keeping it pending indefinitely
x: A pocket veto consists of taking no action—neither assent, rejection nor return—thereby keeping the Bill pending indefinitely.
tq: Distinguish inaction from express rejection and from the suspensive return of a Bill.

s: The possibility of a pocket veto by the President arises principally because:
o: the President has a constitutional power to dissolve Parliament
the Supreme Court authorises indefinite withholding of assent
Article 111 prescribes no time limit for presidential action on a Bill
Money Bills are valid for only ten days
x: Article 111 does not prescribe a time limit for the President's action, unlike the ten-day rule referred to in the United States context.
tq: Identify the constitutional omission that creates the practical power.

s: The only instance of a pocket veto at the Union level is associated with which President and which Bill?
o: Dr. Rajendra Prasad — Indian Telegraph Bill
Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed — Indian Post Office Bill
A.P.J. Abdul Kalam — Prevention of Terrorism Bill
Zail Singh — Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill
x: President Zail Singh used the pocket veto in 1986 in relation to the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill.
tq: Combine the office-holder, year and Bill to defeat near-name distractors.

s: Which statement correctly reflects the present constitutional position concerning a Governor's alleged pocket veto?
o: The Governor has the same indefinite pocket veto as the President.
The Governor has no pocket veto; indefinite inaction under Article 200 is justiciable.
The Governor may keep a Bill pending indefinitely without judicial scrutiny.
The Governor can exercise a pocket veto only over Money Bills.
x: The Supreme Court held in 2025 that indefinite inaction by the Governor under Article 200 is justiciable; therefore, the Governor does not possess a presidential-style pocket veto.
tq: Discriminate between the President's textual time-gap and the Governor's reviewable inaction.

s: Which of the following correctly describes the President's power over a Money Bill passed by Parliament?
o: The President must reject it if it was introduced on prior recommendation.
The President may return it for reconsideration but cannot reject it.
The President has no role after passage by Parliament.
The President may ratify or reject it, but cannot return it for reconsideration.
x: In relation to a Money Bill, the President may assent or withhold assent but cannot return it for reconsideration. Such Bills are generally introduced with prior recommendation.
tq: Use the Money Bill exception to the general return power under Article 111.
sec: Veto over money and constitutional amendment bills

s: With reference to a Constitutional Amendment Bill passed by Parliament, which one of the following is correct?
o: The President may reject it by absolute veto.
The President may return it once for reconsideration.
The President must give assent under the 24th Amendment, 1971.
The President may refer it to the Governor for advice.
x: The 24th Amendment, 1971 made presidential assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill mandatory; the President cannot reject or return it.
tq: Remember the special constitutional-amendment exception to presidential veto powers.
sec: Veto over money and constitutional amendment bills

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Returning a Bill for reconsideration is a one-time power of the President.
2. Financial Bills of Category I and Category II may be returned for reconsideration.
3. The President may return a Constitutional Amendment Bill for reconsideration.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: The return power is one-time and may apply to Financial Bills of Categories I and II. A Constitutional Amendment Bill cannot be returned because assent is mandatory.
tq: Spot the special exception for Constitutional Amendment Bills among otherwise returnable Bills.
sec: Veto over money and constitutional amendment bills

s: A Bill passed by a State Legislature and reserved by the Governor for the consideration of the President is governed primarily by:
o: Article 123
Article 161
Article 201
Article 111
x: Article 201 deals with Bills reserved by the Governor for the consideration of the President.
tq: Match the constitutional Article with the stage at which a State Bill reaches the President.
sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

s: Under Article 200, the Governor must reserve a Bill for the consideration of the President when the Bill:
o: is a Money Bill passed by the State Legislature
has been passed unanimously by the State Legislature
endangers the position of the High Court
relates to a matter in the State List
x: The Governor must reserve a Bill that endangers the position of the High Court. Reservation is otherwise one of the constitutional choices available under Article 200.
tq: Identify the mandatory reservation case rather than an optional or unrelated category.
sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

s:
After a State Bill is reserved for the President's consideration under Article 201, which of the following powers does the President possess?
1. Assent to the Bill
2. Withhold assent
3. Direct the Governor to return a non-money Bill to the State Legislature
4. Remain bound to assent if the State Legislature repasses the Bill
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
x: The President may assent, withhold assent or direct return of a non-money Bill. The President is not bound to assent even if the State Legislature repasses it, making statement 4 false.
tq: Separate the President's Article 201 choices from the binding-assent rule applicable to an ordinary non-money Bill under Article 111.
sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

s: The President's power under Article 201 over a State Bill reserved by the Governor is regarded as an absolute veto because:
o: the President is not bound to assent even when the State Legislature repasses the Bill
the President can dissolve the State Legislature
the Governor cannot communicate with the President
the President can amend the Bill without legislative approval
x: Unlike the ordinary suspensive veto over a non-money parliamentary Bill, the President is not bound to assent to a reserved State Bill even after repassage.
tq: Compare the consequence of repassage under Article 201 with the ordinary suspensive veto.
sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

s: Under Article 201, the State Legislature is required to reconsider a non-money Bill returned by the President within:
o: six months
three months
one year
four months
x: Article 201 provides that the State Legislature should reconsider a non-money Bill returned by the President within six months.
tq: Recall the specific reconsideration period attached to a reserved State Bill.
sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

s: Which sequence correctly reflects the major developments concerning reserved Bills in Tamil Nadu described in the recent constitutional litigation?
o: Presidential Reference opinion — Supreme Court deemed assent — withholding of assent to anti-NEET Bill
Withholding of assent to anti-NEET Bill — Supreme Court deemed assent to ten repassed Bills — Presidential Reference opinion
Supreme Court deemed assent — withholding of assent to anti-NEET Bill — Presidential Reference opinion
Withholding of assent to anti-NEET Bill — Presidential Reference opinion — Supreme Court deemed assent
x: The sequence was withholding of assent to Tamil Nadu's anti-NEET Bill, the April 2025 Supreme Court order deeming ten repassed Bills assented using Article 142, and the November 2025 Presidential Reference opinion rejecting deemed assent as impermissible.
tq: Arrange the litigation by its dated stages and distinguish the later clarifying opinion from the earlier order.
sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

s: What was the significant holding of the Supreme Court in State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu, as described in the constitutional developments of April 2025?
o: It abolished the Governor's power to reserve Bills.
It held that the President must assent to every repassed State Bill.
It held that all gubernatorial inaction is non-justiciable.
Using Article 142, it deemed ten repassed Bills to have received assent and set timelines.
x: In April 2025, the Supreme Court used Article 142 to deem ten repassed Tamil Nadu Bills assented and set timelines.
tq: Identify the unusual remedial action and the constitutional provision used by the Court.
sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

s: According to the Presidential Reference opinion of November 2025 under Article 143, which of the following statements is correct?
o: Courts may always prescribe fixed timelines for constitutional authorities.
Courts cannot fix timelines or grant deemed assent, although prolonged unexplained inaction may receive limited judicial review.
The President has no role in Bills reserved under Article 201.
Deemed assent is constitutionally permissible whenever a Governor delays action.
x: The November 2025 opinion stated that courts cannot fix timelines and that deemed assent is impermissible. It recognised limited review of prolonged unexplained inaction.
tq: Distinguish the later Presidential Reference position from the superseded approach in the earlier litigation.
sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

s: Which recent development revived the debate on the possible misuse of the ordinance-making power and executive overreach?
o: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026
The National Judicial Appointments Ordinance, 2026
The Inter-State Water Disputes Amendment Ordinance, 2026
The Parliamentary Privileges Amendment Ordinance, 2026
x: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 revived the debate on ordinance misuse and executive overreach.
tq: Identify the precise recent development instead of being misled by similarly worded legislative titles.

s: What is the principal criticism of the frequent promulgation of ordinances?
o: They can be issued only during a financial emergency.
They require prior approval from the Supreme Court.
They bypass parliamentary deliberation.
They transfer all legislative powers to the States.
x: Frequent ordinances are criticised because they bypass parliamentary deliberation.
tq: Link the institutional criticism to the constitutional function being bypassed.

s: With reference to the veto power of the President of the United States, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: It is a pocket veto that can be overridden by a simple majority of Congress.
It is a suspensive veto that automatically becomes ineffective after thirty days.
It is a qualified veto that can be overridden by a two-thirds majority of Congress.
It is an absolute veto that cannot be overridden by Congress.
x: The US President has only a qualified veto, which can be overridden by a two-thirds majority of Congress.
tq: Discriminate between absolute, qualified, suspensive and pocket vetoes by focusing on the override condition.

s: The State ordinance concerning organ-transplant committees in Andhra Pradesh was issued under which Article of the Constitution?
o: Article 123
Article 243G
Article 214
Article 213
x: A Governor's ordinance-making power for a State is exercised under Article 213; the Andhra Pradesh ordinance concerned organ-transplant committees.
tq: Use the Union ordinance–State ordinance distinction to identify the correct constitutional Article.

s:
Consider the following statements regarding ordinance-making powers:
1. The Union ordinance-making power is associated with Article 123.
2. The ordinance-making power of a State is associated with Article 213.
3. Frequent promulgation of ordinances has been criticised for bypassing parliamentary deliberation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Statements 1 and 2 correctly identify the Union and State ordinance provisions, respectively. Statement 3 correctly states the principal criticism of frequent ordinances; therefore, all three statements are correct.
tq: Combine the Article distinction with the institutional criticism and check whether all three statements follow the constitutional comparison.
